meta.caveats: Fuel and toll figures are sourced; freight rates are cost-built estimates (diesel + tolls + driver + EMI/depreciation + tyres/maintenance + 10-15% margin) cross-checked against national ranges (Rs 22-40/km for 16-20 t trucks in 2025 blogs; CMIE Delhi-origin 15 t lanes). Grain flows are scaled from Punjab totals using Moga's historical ~6-7% share.

fuel.notes: Moga retail prices (The Core). 2026 rises: Rs 3/L on 15 May + 0.90 on 19 May (crude/Hormuz disruption, weak rupee), more later; Moga petrol was Rs 96.60 a year earlier (Oct 2025). Chandigarh is ~Rs 6/L cheaper on diesel due to lower VAT, so trucks on Moga-tricity lanes fill up in Chandigarh. Some aggregators wrongly show Rs 89.47 for 'Punjab' - that is the Chandigarh price.

unionDynamics: Until 2017, every Punjab town had a truck operators' union (134 statewide) that ran a 'bari' (turn) system: only member trucks could load in its area, freight was fixed by the union, and outside trucks were blocked; industry bodies said union rates were 50-60% above open-market rates, and unions doubled as political muscle. The Congress government notified the Punjab Goods Carriages (Regulation and Prevention of Cartelisation) Rules, 2017, dissolving the unions and giving Regional Transport Authorities power to fix tariff bands; Amarinder Singh refused to roll it back in Jul 2017 despite strikes, highway blockades and truck burnings (e.g. Nakodar), citing High Court judgments. Compliance was patchy: e.g. the Abohar union kept allotting trucks in defiance of the DC; in Apr 2018 unions boycotted grain-transport tenders, forcing the state to let arhtiyas/shellers bid. In Dec 2021 Kejriwal promised to revive unions; the outgoing Congress government issued a revival notification on 7 Jan 2022 just before the model code, opposed by Mohali Industries Association, CICU and FOPSIA. Unions de facto persist in many towns under AAP-era leadership contests (e.g. Bhawanigarh union split, NH blocked, Apr 2026). Model as: local trucking market with a probability-weighted cartel (in Moga a union-coordinated 'bari' likely still governs mandi/sheller loads; open market governs FMCG/industrial loads to tricity). Cartel markup 20-50% on local loads; enforcement weak; periodic strikes in procurement season.
transportTenderNotes: Mandi-to-storage transport and mandi labour for wheat/paddy are awarded annually by the Punjab Department of Food, Civil Supplies & Consumer Affairs via cluster-wise open e-tenders under the yearly Punjab Food Grains Transportation Policy (e.g. 2022 policy: open competitive tendering, security Rs 5/MT of cluster capacity). Bids are quoted as a % over the Schedule of Rates (SOR) that FCI reimburses; in 2018 the state capped premiums at 120% over SOR, prompting a union boycott; where no valid bids come after three attempts, arhtiyas and rice shellers may bid and the Mandi Board fixes per-quintal-per-km rates. CAG (2015) criticised Punjab's flat per-quintal rates that ignored distance versus Haryana's per-qtl-per-km schedule. Labour (unloading, cleaning, weighing, filling, stitching, loading) is paid per bag (paddy Rs 17.50 -> 19.26/37.5 kg bag after a 10% hike; unions cite Rs 16.05/35 kg bag) through arhtiyas/contractors, with wages required via RTGS/PF; palledars allege they get ~Rs 2 of a Rs 5/bag entitlement. Transport bills are paid by agencies after delivery verification, often with multi-month lags, so contractors need working capital from arhtiyas or banks.
